blueprint_concepts: Divisibility and remainder problems using binomial expansion
Last digit and last two digits problems
english: The number of positive integers $n\le150$ for which $11^{n}+9^{n}$ is divisible by $100$ is ______.
solution: So $n$ is an odd multiple of $5$: $5,15,\dots,145$, i.e. $15$ values
solution_full: For even $n$: $9^{n}\equiv1-10n$, so $11^{n}+9^{n}\equiv2\pmod{100}$. The last two digits are $02$; never divisible by $100$.
For odd $n$: $9^{n}\equiv-1+10n$, so $11^{n}+9^{n}\equiv20n\pmod{100}$. This is $0$ modulo $100$ iff $100\mid20n$, i.e. $5\mid n$.
So the condition is: $n$ odd and $5\mid n$, i.e. $n\equiv5\pmod{10}$. In $1\le n\le150$: $n=5,15,25,\dots,145$, which is $\dfrac{145-5}{10}+1=15$ values.
originality_note: New: the last two digits of 11^n + 9^n are found for all n at once from (10 +- 1)^n, giving 02 for even n and 20n mod 100 for odd n, and the divisible cases are then counted (way 2, a family analysed as a function of n). Closest known: last two digits of 11^n or remainder of 9^n mod 100 for one n. Different because: the parity split and the count over a range are the point.

concept_use.Divisibility and remainder problems usin: Divisibility of 11^n + 9^n by 100 is decided from the binomial expansions of (1+10)^n and (10-1)^n.
concept_use.Last digit and last two digits problems: The last two digits are 02 for even n and those of 20n for odd n.
concept_use.Remainder based problems: The remainder of 11^n + 9^n on division by 100 is computed as 2 or 20n mod 100.

stem_review: Read as a student: n ranges over positive integers up to 150 inclusive, divisibility by 100 is unambiguous; answer 15 is a positive 2-digit integer as planned (brute-force checked); Hindi mirrors. No change.
key_step: Get the residues modulo 100 for even and odd n from (10 +- 1)^n and see that 5 | n is needed for odd n.
justification: Two-case analysis of a family of remainders followed by a count; numerical with a parity trap. Comparable to L3 counting anchors such as 2026-P1-Q11 (L3).
